extracted.intended_audience: aspiring performers, open-mic hosts/organizers, and general readers interested in open mic events
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and norms for running and performing at open mic nights across comedy, music, and poetry—covering sign-up, timing, host duties, stage setup, etiquette, and format variants. Useful for novice performers and venue hosts organizing open-mic events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign-up and screening procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Performers may sign up in advance for a time slot with the host, who is typically an experienced performer or the venue's manager or owner. The host may screen potential candidates for suitability for the venue and give them a time to perform during the show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hosts commonly use a sign-up list; systems vary by venue. Screening is used to ensure suitability for the venue and to organize the running order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microphone and amplification requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: As the name suggests, performers are usually provided with a microphone plugged into a PA system so that they can be better heard by the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stand-up performances have a designated stage area and use a microphone with amplification as an industry standard. Minimal technical setup is expected for most open-mic formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits per act and timing signals
rubrics_metrics.description: At a typical comedy open mic, acts will get 3–7 minutes of stage time. The host will flash a light at the comedian one minute before their time is up as a signal to finish the joke they are currently telling, a practice known as 'getting the light.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five-minute slots require ~three minutes of material. Modern practice uses a cell phone flashlight to signal one minute left. Ignoring the light ('blowing the light') may get the comedian banned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show length and number of acts
rubrics_metrics.description: An open mic night should be no longer than 90 minutes and consist of no more than 15 acts. A comedy open mic will not normally exceed 30 people in the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits maintain audience energy and keep the show concise; these numbers are cited as common norms rather than strict rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality requirement for stand-up
rubrics_metrics.description: All stand-up comedy performed must be an original creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original material is a central norm of modern stand-up; joke stealing is noted as one of the most grievous offenses a stand-up can commit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host/MC responsibilities and qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The host is typically an experienced performer or venue manager who introduces acts, warms up the audience, maintains an equilibrium of mood within 'the room', seats audience members to maximize enjoyment, and may screen performers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hosts may be paid and sometimes perform during the evening. The MC's duties include contextualization, framing of response, evaluation, request for action (applause), and introduction. Good hosts help sustain audience energy between acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience composition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience for a typical comedy open mic is other comedians; audience cooperation allows the act to succeed and they retain the right to undermine the interaction by withdrawing that cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seats arranged close to the front can increase feelings of a 'full house' and audience responsiveness. Reading the room (gauging demographics and affective response) is vital for performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lineup strategy and performer preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing first at an open mic puts the comedian at a disadvantage due to the audience being 'cold'; comics should show up a few acts ahead to 'read' the audience and may use open mics to test or refine material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comics often attend other sets to observe. More experienced comedians use open mics to work out new characters or material; novices should practice brevity (3–5 minutes) and icebreakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage setup and minimal staging
rubrics_metrics.description: Staging for stand-up is minimal—typically a stool, a microphone stand, and a neutral backdrop (blank wall or curtain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The minimal setup is part of the genre's accessibility: virtually anyone can perform without specialized gear or credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etiquette around time and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: If a performer goes over their time limit or ignores the one-minute light, this is known as 'blowing the light' and may get them banned. Staying onstage longer than allotted time and joke stealing are among the most grievous offenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hosts will diplomatically intervene if a performer exceeds time. Respecting time slots and fellow performers' material is essential to maintaining good standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formats: show-and-go, booked shows, bringer shows
rubrics_metrics.description: Open mics have variants: 'show and go' (no minimum requirements—just show up and put your name on the list), booked shows (reserve spots in advance), and 'bringer shows' (each performer must bring a set number of people to secure stage time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bringer shows commonly require bringing 5–15 people and are widely seen as exploitative. Choose formats mindful of fairness and venue goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host as gatekeeper for poetry/spoken word
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and spoken word open mics feature a host (normally a poet) who acts as a 'gatekeeper', determining which performers are suitable; a sign-up sheet is generally available for anyone interested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants are asked to keep to specified time slots; if they go over, the host diplomatically thanks them and asks them to yield the stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical open-mic arrangements (house band/blues night)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some music open mics use a house band (e.g., 'Blues Night') so singers/instrumentalists sign up to play with a band; songs chosen are usually simple blues standards and may be announced by form/key ('12-bar fast shuffle in C').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: House-band formats require the host to screen and order performers and to coordinate keys/arrangements so unfamiliar musicians can play together without rehearsal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording performances for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: It is common practice for stand-ups to record their sets for later review and rehearsal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedians are advised to record every set, listen back, and transcribe material they wish to keep. Collective audience feedback across shows shapes routine development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience warm-up and framing by the compere
rubrics_metrics.description: The compere/MC warms up the audience to 'train' them how to respond—establishing comic license, creating group consensus for laughter, and orienting the audience to the nature of the routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rutter identifies compere turns: contextualization, framing of response, evaluation, request for action, introduction, and audience applause. Effective warm-up reduces audience inhibition to laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer introduction etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: The host introduces each act by reciting the name placed on the sign-up list and asks the audience to give the performer an introductory round of applause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introductions help orient the audience and provide a polite transition onto the stage; they also serve to establish expectations for the performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of group acts and logistical limits
rubrics_metrics.description: It is less common for groups such as rock bands or comedy troupes to perform at open mics because of space and logistical requirements for equipment and soundchecking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open mics generally favor solo or small acoustic acts; venues should assess space and technical capacity before allowing group performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience size and room dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical arrangement and audience size influence enjoyment—tightly arranged seating near the stage can create the 'feeling of a full house' and increase laughter; larger or sparser arrangements reduce communal responsiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hosts can manipulate seating and staging to maximize audience involvement and create a safer environment for collective laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and benefits for performers
rubrics_metrics.description: Open mics provide networking, exposure, and experience—novices gain stage time, watch others work, practice stage presence, and connect with seasoned performers for advice and future opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers should view open mics as learning environments and networking opportunities; organizers can emphasize these benefits when recruiting participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement and diplomatic intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Hosts act diplomatically if performers exceed time limits or behave inappropriately, e.g., thanking an overlong poet and asking them to yield the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining goodwill while enforcing rules is important; escalation (bans for repeated offenses like blowing the light or theft) may be applied by venues.
